utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you. Madam Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric, and good morning to you. You may be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. In my team also is Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with John Jones I appear here today, and with our legal assistant Ms. Adisa Mehic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Yesterday, in your absence, Mr. Wubben, we had some submissions on the -- on our indication that we will be proceeding with appointing our own handwriting expert, and I of course reserved -- since you were not here at the time, I told Ms. Sellers that we'll wait until your return. I suggest that if you have submissions to make on this, we will leave them until the end of the sitting, and we'll try first to finish with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, waiting for the end of the sitting today will mean that I'm not able to attend to a meeting with our -- with our advisor regarding this issue. I have a meeting scheduled at around 12.00. So if it is possible then to make the submissions in that respect tomorrow morning, first start, or at the end of the session tomorrow, then that will suit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right with us. I suppose with the Defence it doesn't make a difference. Okay. So you'll make the submissions tomorrow and you will have the -- rather, we will all have the advantage of your having first consulted with your advisors. All right. Any other preliminaries before we start with the witness? Please keep them as short as possible so that -- I want to make sure that this witness is out of here today. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will keep it short. To update the Trial Chamber that we are continuing organising our rebuttal, we updated you that we had candidates for that. One of those witnesses is not able to attend in the specific week starting the 31st of January due to the fact that he's abroad. He can only come in to start giving evidence on the 6th of February. And in addition to the -- these candidate witnesses, I learned from yesterday that the Defence intend to file a motion with a view to the admittance of the interviews of the accused and that that might have a consequence also to advocate that, as a kind of poisoned fruit, the signatures put by the accused are also affected. That means for us that we reserve from yesterday our right also in rebuttal to give evidence via witnesses in that respect. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But we still haven't got an indication of how many witnesses you're bringing over in rebuttal with this caveat, because I can quite understand what your preoccupation is, but forget this reservation that you have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And assuming that you will get also this witness that, in Manzonian terms, would be the unnamed, the innominata. Where do we stand? I mean, how much time do you need? I really don't care to know for the time being precisely the names, because that's more of the concern of the Defence than of us, but I want -- and we came here early this morning to discuss with our staff several organisational issues. We need to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: For three out of the four witnesses, a rough estimation is five days, and then in addition, the possibility of Docterandus Fagel, but that should be discussed within the team after the testimony of Bilic, and we are quite aware that the Trial Chamber -- of the possibility to include such questions also within the request to the Trial Chamber expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see anyway, but please by the end of the week we need to have in black on white the indication of who you want to call in rebuttal, with the time you estimate you need for the testimony in chief, so that we will have feedback from the Defence. And of course for the time being, I can't -- I can't even ask the Defence what they -- what they plan. There will be a reservation, of course, on this matter relating to the interview if that matter comes up. If you want to bring forward evidence on that, of course you can make the application to the Trial Chamber and we will decide whether to accept it or not. But of course we are reserving your rights for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's the position. Any further preliminaries on our part?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On your part, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only wish to briefly turn to what Mr. Wubben said and comment upon it and then we will have two or three questions. Based on what my learned colleague Wubben said this morning, I can see that they already have names. They already know who the persons are who they will invite for rebuttal, and I believe it would have been fair for them to inform us of the names of these persons as soon as they knew them. What we expect from them now is to receive statements in order for us to prepare our defence and our cross-examination of these witnesses. I wish to state here that the Prosecutor could not have been surprised by the fact that we were finishing our case in January. We were trying to strictly adhere to the order issued by this Honourable Trial Chamber, which stated that the case should be finished by the end of January. This had been planned long ago, and we should have had the names a long time ago if we want to have a fair trial. That's why we expect to receive the statements as soon as possible. Your Honours, I have to address you this morning on another matter as well. You will recall that yesterday the Prosecution addressed the Chamber in relation to P598, their own Prosecution exhibit. They wanted to replace their P598 with another document because they stated that the front page and some other pages were missing. I am indeed content with the fact that we had -- we reacted yesterday and that you refused to grant the replacement before we take a look at it. Yesterday we carefully reviewed the document and came to a highly -- to a conclusion that is of great concern to us. I will not address the matter of disclosure at this stage, although it should be, but I do not have the time. If need be, we may submit a detailed analysis of the disclosure matter to the Chamber as well. However, there is another matter which is of far greater concern to us and I wish it to be stated for the record for the sake of the further proceedings. The document which Madam Prosecutor asked to be replaced yesterday because she stated that the front page had been missing, I have to note that -- that the page which is the front page of the document is the one bearing the ERN number 04231845 and it was already contained in the document. I believe this is a highly pressing matter, and I would wish the paper that we prepared to be distributed here. Therefore, the page number 04231845, when you glance at it you can see that the first page has number 1 in the upper right corner, and as you flip through the document - we haven't gone page by page but I believe that this is the case - if you look at the subsequent pages, 2, 3, 4, 5, through to 54, they run through to 54, the page the Prosecutor wanted to submit, which was the one carrying the number 02995208, at first sight even a person who is a layman can see that there is a very rough alteration of names, or even retracing of names, and you will see that these are the names of Kemal Mehmedovic and Senad Golubovic, names which had been repeatedly mentioned in this case. I wish to draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that the first page of this document is not the one that is listed as number 1 in EDS, but instead the page on the EDS bears the number 02995207, where it is stated that three war diaries were received with attorney-at-law Mr. Petrusic from Belgrade. This, however, was not submitted here for admission. Now, please take a look at page number 02995208, the one that the Prosecutor wanted to submit. Fifth line from the bottom. If you look at that line and then through to the end of the page, where it says Tabakovic Mirsad, 10 January 1994, and then compare this item with page 1 of Exhibit P598. From document P598, those important names of Kemal Mehmedovic and Senad Golubovic are missing, as well as are some others that were written in the other text, including the dates and everything else that we were supposed to discuss with our witnesses. I don't think the Prosecutor should refer to the EDS and the text that is there because I assert that the document is a completely different one. It doesn't bear any page marks, and to me it is a totally different document. The Prosecutor was using only this P598. The last time it was used was with Witness D005, and that was after the time the document was placed on the EDS. Your Honours, another matter which I deem is most important is as follows, but first I want to direct your attention to the fact that this portion of the text on the page that you were looking at, which was tendered here, this particular text was photocopied three times, and then number 1 was added to it, and this was supposed to be page 1 of document P598. However, what I find is of most grave concern and gives rise to suspicion is the name added, Himzo Hodzic, as well as the names that are missing and are contained on page 02995208, which was offered by the Prosecutor yesterday to be -- to replace the other page. This person Popovic, or somebody else, if they appear here as Prosecution witnesses, this will constitute something that goes beyond the scope of what is allowed in all the criminal procedures, and we will try to prevent this. Not only were we prevented or hindered from showing these documents to the witnesses who were participants in these events, we were also prevented from pointing to all the details concerning the names and dates mentioned on the allegedly missing papers because the papers had been thus manipulated. Your Honours, whenever we receive such a document, we analyse and examine every single detail contained in the document. We make searches with regard to the persons mentioned, to the authors, to the whereabouts of the persons, whether they were actually there where it was mentioned. We were unable to do so. Again it will be said that this was a technical error, it was an error that occurred during photocopying; however, if this happens once more, I will not be able to be persuaded that this was in fact an error. We cannot be prevented from preparing the defence for our client at this late stage in the proceedings because, Your Honours, we have had numerous such errors in the case so far. We appeal to you, Your Honours, to prevent the rights of our accused -- of the accused be infringed. He is looking to you to prevent this. And one day there will be a written record of all that we have been doing, of our conduct in this case. Your Honour, at this stage we demand that the Prosecutor not only give us access to the original of this document, but also that the original be handed to our expert, Professor Bilic, who is here, to examine the document. Your Honour, I want to correct the record. I said that if this -- I see that the record says this person Popovic. I said Mr. Himzo Hodzic instead of Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sellers, do you want to comment on this, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. I certainly do want to comment. I think Madam Vidovic has brought out several issues that the Prosecutor has alluded to in a much more discreet manner. First of all, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Usher -- where is the usher? Please go and tell the witness that we are taking some time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go and inform the witness and apologise to her, saying that we are discussing some procedural issues that do not relate to her and that we will call her as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try and be as brief as possible. First of all, in response to Madam Vidovic's last request, they have already made a request to the Prosecution to produce the original and the Prosecution is right now in the process of contacting evidence unit so that this original can be produced to them. In terms of having Dr. Bilic examine this, if he is doing it in informal consultation with Defence counsel, that's one thing. If it's going to be part of any type of expertise, I would then remind the Court that there's been no Rule 94 bis submission. So my understanding would be that Madam Vidovic is talking about an informal consultation with him. Might I say right away that the number 1 that Madam Vidovic has pointed out on the page of 598, that that was put there by our investigator because when -- and that's the entire problem that we were talking about in terms of analysing the document that we've placed on the record. We were -- we had a document where this appeared as a first page and we had information and it did not make sense that this was the first page, and therefore for reasons of the first page having three different types of repeat on it, having information, because we had asked for information concerning this document, knowing that there was other information on a first page. I really do not want to go into these details, they are very much the work product that we have been alluding to, in my view. I wouldn't want to present a document that we ourselves felt was not complete to your witnesses in cross-examination. We were finally able to understand that we had had the document, and after we clarified to ourselves that document, which now contains what we believe is the real first page and the missing pages, it is only at that time, and very much to the detriment of the case of the Prosecution, that we have come forward with this. I understand completely in terms of what the Defence is saying of potential prejudice, but we thought it would be much more misleading and inaccurate to continue to say that 598 was the integral document. I do want to repeat some other things. In terms of what appears to be rewriting on the front of the page, the Prosecution is not in any way stating and certainly not concurring with the Defence as how to this writing, rewriting occurred. I think that's a matter for evidence, that's matter that might come before your Trial Chambers, but certainly it is not a matter of conjecture. If it is a matter of expertise that Dr. Bilic would have a statement upon, we just ask the Defence do that in the proper way. We want to use this document. That is the reason that we have asked that it be substituted, and certainly obey the Trial Chamber's decision not to have it substituted but to come in in a proper method. We certainly want the Defence to look at the originals and the Trial Chamber to look at the original. We do not necessarily want the Defence to delay beyond what is reasonable in examining this so that there would be no witnesses in which to show the document to. Your Honour, if there are any other questions concerning this document, concerning what would be the work product connected with this document, I would suggest in open court that we file something ex parte with you because the work product of the Prosecution is not necessarily meant for the public domain or for the information of the Defence. If it is something that the Trial Chamber rightly feels that we should serve or share with the Defence, we certainly do not mind filing that in a manner which is confidential. We will be renewing our request to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the best thing is -- would be to stop the discussion on this here. If you have things to iron out, clothes to iron out amongst ourselves on this and to clarify between yourselves on this, please do so during the break. We'll, of course, discuss amongst ourselves the submissions that you have made. It's not something that I can comment here and now upon without consultation with my two -- with my two colleagues, and will come back to you, and if -- when and if. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one preliminary which I feel I have to mention as well, so perhaps I can mention that now and then I can also say one thing about P598 in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise to my colleague. I just wish you to know that the Prosecutor had this document on the EDS in July 2005, and there is nothing further for us to discuss with them. If they had it on the EDS and they knew about this in 2005, I don't understand why it was not disclosed to us in July 2005. Your Honours, you can see that every day strange things are happening, and this is being allowed to go. We wish to bring this trial to conclusion within the boundaries of what is fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to continue this, and I do agree that we -- Prosecution still stands with a channel of open discussion with Defence on this document. I would not like to think that we arrived at a point where we cannot discuss this issue. In terms of disclosure of this issue, we have found that this was part of a disclosure that was, if I understand correctly, was part of a G binder that we have written several motions on in the recent past, explaining either failure to disclosure or when it was disclosed. In looking at that disclosure is when the Prosecution finally understood the existence and integrity of the document and immediately made plans not only to use it but to turn it over. I believe that those issues of disclosure have been taken care of in another form. Right now I think the issue is not just disclosure and not primarily disclosure but the ability of the Prosecution to use the document and for the Defence to use the document or to contest the document. In terms of the failure to not understand that the entire document was there, I do have to emphasise and that is in no way an excuse of any disclosure irresponsibility, although I think that the Trial Chamber's addressed it, is that other than the three or four pages that we have stood up openly in court and explained that we're missing, that the Defence was not only completely aware of this document but my learned friends made vociferous arguments against the document the first time it was to be used. Your Honours, we can continue this among the parties. I believe that that would be the most productive way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, my preliminary is going to be different one. It concerns the scheduling for Lieutenant Colonel Fenzel, and a problem has arisen with regard to him coming next week, I regret to say. And just by way of background, we have had contacts with the witness for a long time but it was only -- it was only recently and in fact during the proofing of Lieutenant Colonel Dudley when we had contacts with the USG, the American government, that it became clear that actually our contacts had to be regulated or re-regulated through that government, which meant a new request to contact the witness, to interview him, and also a request for a Rule 70 order from the Trial Chamber. Due to the Christmas break and recent holidays, including Martin Luther King Day recently, we could only have the interview yesterday, and I -- I made them aware, of course, our schedule from the start, that we wanted to have Lieutenant Colonel Fenzel here next week, but firstly the US government is now, due partly, I have to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need to stay in public session or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I don't think -- dealings with governments I don't think are the concern of the public at this stage. When they become so, of course I will go into public -- we'll go into open session. Yes, let's go -- you agree I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while we're waiting, I suppose it's really to bring out obvious point that if the Trial Chamber appointed expert were a member of an institute organised in the European network of forensic science institutes, then we might have a problem because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but listen, you can have as many problems as you like. The choice of the expert is our own responsibility and concern, not yours. No one bothered you when you chose your own expert or when Mr. Wubben chose his own expert, and we will choose our own expert, and then if you want to contest to our own expert if he is a member or she is a member of this, then you're free to suggest to him that this is the policy that this lady indicates in this letter. But otherwise, please don't interfere with who we wish to -- to appoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you are feeling better, and I apologise to you for having kept you waiting in the room there, but we had several issues to discuss which are not related to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to do our best to try and finish with your testimony today. Let's hope we will. I'm sure that the parties will cooperate to their utmost. Yes. Ms. Sellers will now continue with -- with her examination -- with her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We are going to do our utmost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. My apologies to the usher, because right now we have the ELMO that, when I'm standing up, is completely blocking Ms. Djilovic's face. I will start asking questions while you're doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Djilovic.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask today because of the -- what's going to be quite crucial time constraints, that if you could keep your answers as brief as possible, that would assist us, and I in no way want to indicate that the Prosecution does not want to hear what you have to say, but I would like to convey to you that I believe that both the Prosecution but, more important, the Trial Chamber understands the context of the situation of Srebrenica in those days, and therefore when you are answering questions, we will have the context of your situation as a -- as an understandable background so you need not explain that at times to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask that P4 be placed in front of the witness. That's where we left off yesterday. And at the same time could I ask that D986 be placed in front of the witness, and I believe that that will facilitate the examination. Yes. It's D986 and P4. P4, I understand, is on Sanction. I'm trying to use the Defence exhibit because I believe possibly the witness will be more familiar with it since it was used during proofing and at the session. And D986 I understand was the handwritten document that the Defence used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I have never seen this document. I don't remember this. The protocol is unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Madam --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may. Under 10, it says here, "TO staff." As far as I know, under 10, the services attached to the Srebrenica TO couldn't have been there. If there was a staff I didn't know about, I don't know, but as far as I know, there was no TO staff in 1992. The war hospital, the signals and information service, the military police, all this is under 10, A, B and C. All these services were attached to the municipal War Presidency, and they could in no way have been attached to a TO staff of Srebrenica that I know nothing about. I know very well that all these three institutions were attached to the municipal executive board. Avdo Hasanovic, I remember well, was in charge of the hospital. Hamed Alic in charge of information. And as for this military police, which I always felt was actually a civilian police, the person in charge was Mirzet Halilovic. That's what I know about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers, because for -- in the record we have given the impression that P4 is on Sanction. In actual fact there is nothing on Sanction, at least on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I see it on our screen. There might have been a technical difficulty. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is on the ELMO, but it's not on Sanction. It's the other one that you have to press, Judge Eser, the second one on the left. The one in the middle. Yeah, that one. It is now, yes. It is now on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mrs. Djilovic, my question to you -- and thank you for that information. My question to you under the services attached to the Srebrenica TO is that to your knowledge, as you've just testified, you're unaware that there were any services attached to the TO. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I didn't even know there was a TO staff in 1992. I'm not aware of that at all. I'm not aware of its existence at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. And, Madam Djilovic, that just means that in terms of Hamed Alic being attached to a TO staff, you would just simply agree with me that you weren't aware of that; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was aware, yeah. No, no. I know that he was in charge of the information service, and this service belonged to the municipal War Presidency, not to the TO staff, because as far as I know, there wasn't a TO staff in existence at that time. That's all I know about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment, Judge Eser, because I had noticed Ms. Vidovic standing. Maybe you can --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has clarified what she clearly stated before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thought so much, actually, but anyway, let's hear what Judge Eser wishes to state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Perhaps it may be a question of language again. If I read the English version of P4, number 10, it only speaks of Srebrenica TO and not of "TO staff," and I always thought there was a difference between Territorial Defence and Territorial Defence staff. So if you please look -- I think even in the B/C/S version it only speaks of TO Srebrenica, not of TO Srebrenica in something like that. The heading speaks of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Srebrenica TO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But number 10 does not speak of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It only speaks of -- I just ask whether that means something, the difference between "TO staff" and "TO" without "staff."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that whoever drew up this document -- well, I -- I'm not really familiar with Territorial Defence, but in the heading, it says "TO Defence staff," and all these services are supposed to be attached to it. But even had there been just the TO, not the TO staff here, they couldn't have been attached to that either; they could only have been attached to the municipal War Presidency. I don't know if that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Madam Djilovic, would you now look at document D986, which is also in front of you, and do you recall that you looked at that Defence document during your proofing session and also during your direct testimony? Correct, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And when you looked at that list, you noted that these were members of the War Presidency and you testified at that time that Naser Oric, who is on the list, was a member of the War Presidency. Do you remember that, Ms. Djilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Now, you --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the municipal War Presidency, but this document doesn't mean anything to me. It doesn't say who received it or who delivered it. There's no heading. To me, it looks like a copy or a forgery. This is not a proper document, in my view. It doesn't say who is sending it, it doesn't have an addressee. It's more like a draft.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you agree that the information in this document is what you came to know in terms of members of the War Presidency when you joined the Municipal Staff?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. You testified on direct when you looked at this document that the information in the document was correct. Is that your testimony today or would you like to change your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That's correct. When I started working, there was the municipal War Presidency in place. These persons were already in the municipal War Presidency. But what we're talking about now is the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is the information in the document correct to your understanding? I'm talking about the information in the document. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they're correct. These were the members of the municipal War Presidency, the persons listed here, at the time when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. And included in the information on the document that you were shown to by the Defence, it says Naser Oric, and next to it says, "Commander TO."

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've only just noticed this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that there was a Territorial Defence. I wasn't aware of that now. I didn't think, and I don't think that the institution itself of Territorial Defence existed as far as I knew, and I based my knowledge on what I was able to see when I started working. You can see here it says TO, but this doesn't mean anything to me because this has no heading, and I wouldn't consider it to be a document. I don't believe anyone working in the administration would think that this signifies anything. Anybody could have written this. The names are here, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So can I just ask you one brief question, then: In relationship to Naser Oric's name on this document that you were shown by the Defence, you never discussed whether he was a commander of the TO staff or not in relationship to this document?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Naser Oric was never commander of the TO, especially not in 1992. I know that he was always at the front line. Whenever he came to the War Presidency municipal building he was wearing boots and very soon he'd be out again. So he came in, stayed briefly only. I worked for the municipal War Presidency. And as for the Territorial Defence, I don't believe it could have existed, especially not in 1992. But this could also be true for 1993, in view of the general situation in Srebrenica. There were great numbers of refugees, people were confused.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm going to have to ask you to shorten your answers and just answer my next question, please, yes or no. Then do you know why Naser Oric was a member of the War Presidency? Do you know why he was chosen to be a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably just as all the other members, he was elected by -- by the local group leaders, those who were around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. So he would at least have been among the leaders of Srebrenica. That's your testimony. Right, Mrs. Djilovic? Or not. Just say yes or no. Fine.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was not among the leaders, one of the leaders at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have confused me a bit. These members here were members on paper for the most part. They were trying to do what they could to help the refugees and the residents of Srebrenica. Psychologically, it was important to organise something for the sake of the people. When the people heard that there was someone working in the municipality, it made them feel better, and then they had someone to address their needs to for food, fuel, clothing. Whatever was done was done for the sake of the people of Srebrenica. Believe me, Naser Oric did the same, tried to help people, just as Jusuf did, Becir did, Halilovic, Bogilovic; all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies that for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask if those documents could be removed from the witness and the witness could be shown P42.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, the document you have before you is dated the 1st of July, 1992, and if you look through the document, it's a decision to appoint and form members of the War Presidency. I would draw your attention to Article 4, where you see that it says, "The following are hereby appointed members of the War Presidency." And that includes Hajrudin Avdic, Hamdija Fejzic, Resid Efendic, Naser Oric, Dzemaludin Becirevic, Jusuf Halilovic, Becir Bogilovic, Mirsad Dudic, and it continues on the next page, Lefik Mandzic - which I believe might be a misspelling - Aziz Nekic, and Senahid Tabakovic. Now, from your testimony, you would agree that these were persons who became members of the Srebrenica War Presidency; isn't that correct, Ms. Djilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for Senahid Tabakovic, who was not on the municipal War Presidency from the very start. He was appointed member of the War Presidency at a later stage. Therefore, he wasn't there from the start. That is to say Senahid Tabakovic. But the rest, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you also agree that under Article 5 it's correct that Hajrudin Avdic was appointed to be president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, that's correct. I was not working at the time. I came in later. But nevertheless, I know that Senahid Tabakovic wasn't there. Hajrudin Avdic was already president of the municipal War Presidency of Srebrenica. The only thing that is not correct in this document is that Senahid Tabakovic was not there on the 1st of July, but that's as far as I can comment on this; I did not type this out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to ask you that later. But you can also confirm that Resid Efendic, as you testified earlier, became the secretary of the War Presidency? That's under Article 6.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And under Article --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was secretary of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Under Article 7, I assume that you would not have any knowledge that Naser Oric was appointed commander of the armed forces. Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I knew. Well, I cannot give you a yes or no answer, because I really do not know that there was Territorial Defence and that there were some commanders. I really thought at the time that it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Fine. We also understand that sometime you can say yes or no or sometime you do not know, but you do know that, and I'm just going to say, under Article 8, Hamdija Fejzic was appointed to the Executive Committee. I believe you testified about that earlier.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And there are other appointments that, if I look at your testimony concerning Mr. Becirevic, Mr. Bogilovic, and Mr. Halilovic, that you testified that indeed they held these positions in the War Presidency; secretary for the economy, public security station, and civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, they were only members, and it was only later that they were appointed to these posts. That was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, do you by any chance know who was acting in any capacity on the War Presidency whose name is not here?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what time period you have in mind. Are you referring to this list?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me clarify that, and I believe in the transcript I meant whose name. When you arrived at the end of July, was there someone who was on the War Presidency who you don't see in this document?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask this document to be removed and --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could just give me a moment. I believe that Mirzet Halilovic was there as well. I know that Senahid Tabakovic wasn't there, but Mirzet was. I meant Mirzet Halilovic. He was a member of the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for not having grasped that immediately, but it took some time to look at the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That's absolutely fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask that Ms. Djilovic be shown Prosecution Exhibit 109. I believe this is also Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit 270.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that is dated the 2nd of July, 1992, decision -- subject matter is decision.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm going to ask you a question in relationship to it. The decisions of the Territorial Defence Staff of Srebrenica. Now, Ms. Djilovic, I know you've testified that you're unaware, you don't know whether there was a Territorial Defence Staff, and given that testimony that you've just rendered to the Trial Chamber, I did not want to ask you about members on the Territorial staff. I'm asking you about -- not about the existence of the Territorial staff. I'm asking you about references to things that you do know. Therefore, I would like to go to the second paragraph of that document, and it says the War Presidency -- "Since the previous War Presidency had left the territory of the municipality, a new War Presidency was formed ..." Now you would agree a new War Presidency was formed at the beginning of July. Yes or no. This is in accordance with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about these documents, then I'm afraid that I cannot say anything. Everything related to these documents is unknown to me, especially the fact that it says the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence. As far as the Territorial Defence is concerned, there's nothing I can tell you, because I wasn't performing any other duties than those of the -- those that came under the War Presidency. When I look at this document, it seems there's the head -- there's the heading that is a bit strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not answering the question. Ms. Sellers, please rephrase your question. Make it more specific. The witness may have misunderstood you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me withdraw that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go through --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I was trying to explain I'm not talking about the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Let me withdraw the question I asked you and let me ask specifically. Let's go down to the third paragraph in this document, and it says: "A decision was made to form wartime military police; Mirzet Halilovic was appointed commander of this unit." Ms. Djilovic, that is something that you know about and you agree that happened at the beginning -- around this time period, in 1992, in Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you only the following answer: I've already given a lot of information yesterday concerning the military police, and I stand by what I said yesterday, and I'm sorry that I cannot really provide you with anything new in relation to this document because it is unknown to me. As far as military police is concerned, I stand by what I said yesterday. I believe I was clear yesterday. The military police could not have existed because we didn't have an army. It could have existed only on paper. As far as I know, it all came under the civilian police. They all worked together and came to the meetings together. It was only done on paper. It may have been the War Presidency's wish to have all these institutions functioning, however, the entire situation was totally improvised, as I said yesterday. It wasn't properly functioning. It doesn't say who the addressee of the document is, and it seems to me to be sort of a -- a sort of copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Madam Djilovic --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't really look like a document, and I cannot comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm asking about some information in the document, but thank you for your comments on the document. So you don't know whether the military police existed or not. Would that be your testimony? Because I was rather -- I was rather confused by your answer. Can you say yes or no; do you know whether it existed or not?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the military police existed within the civilian police, but it existed on paper rather than in reality. They called it military police, but in fact it worked together with the civilian police. There was no difference between the two. They did the same job, to the best of my knowledge. But I was there, and I was able to see, and that's the only thing I can tell you, what I saw and observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would ask you to go down to the next to last paragraph in this document, where it says, "Hamed Alic was appointed to the chief of this service," and the paragraph above refers to communication and information service. Now, my question is: The last sentence says: "This service has a task to ensure communication with the BH TO Staffs and the Regional Staff, and ensure the rest of the time with families of TO combatants and other citizens." Did you know that Hamed Alic's information communication service was available to both the military and to civilians? Did you know that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Hamed Alic was chief of the communication information service and that he was at the disposal of the entire population in Srebrenica. They were there to provide services to all the people living in Srebrenica. I -- as for the army, I guarantee to you that there was no army in Srebrenica. There were local groups defending their own villages. I'm sorry that I'm unable to provide to you a better answer. I know that he was there to serve all the people who were there. Everything went through the service and through the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We can remove this document from the witness now. I would now ask the witness be shown Defence film on the War Presidency. In just one minute I'll have the number of that exhibit. It's D1003, and it will be in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, this segment of the video, Madam Djilovic, you would agree that that military police was a military police that appeared to be active? It was -- the discussion was preventing shooting, and the discussion was their actions, I believe, in Potocari. Would you agree that this was more than just a paper military police but, according to the War Presidency meeting, an active military police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before she answers, for the record, the witness was shown an extract from this video from 00.00 to 00.27.6.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat it, please? Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. The question I asked - and maybe let me simplify it - from looking at this segment of the video of the War Presidency meeting, would you agree that the military police was a military police that appeared to be active? The discussion was preventing shooting that they did, and they were discussing their actions. It existed more than just on paper.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No actions were involved here. I've said so yesterday, but I can repeat it here again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were discussing Mirzet Halilovic and the shooting at this particular meeting, and you were able to see that. Hajrudin sent Halilovic over to Potocari to see what this was about, because you know that we thought that every single bullet was precious for the population, the civilian population living in the area. He sent him over to see what this was about. This was no action. It was, rather, an intervention on his part to see who was shooting and why. Mirzet Halilovic also worked within the structure of the civilian police. He went out into the field, they wouldn't give him ammunition, and then he beat up one of them. And then what sort of police can this be under such conditions? You have to understand that the situation --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was such --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to maintain answers much shorter. And if you misunderstand me, I was not speaking of actions in what seems to be the terminology of an action being an attack or a battle, I said "active." Maybe there was a misunderstanding. So can I ask you this: Do you think this video is only talking about Mirzet Halilovic and not about the military police?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard what they were saying, but I know what happened and the case that they're discussing. I apologise for having misunderstood you. I thought you were saying that they were going to Potocari into action. I apologise, but I must have misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: My apologies for not having a direct question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be continuing with this video, and I think that maybe we should just continue this after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break now. In the meantime, if you could let us have the Rule 70 motion as early as possible, I'll start working on it straight away, because I think we need to move there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have it here in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: File it, I mean, immediately with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you've missed the point. File it whenever you like, but if you have a courtesy copy of it which you can let me have now, I can start working on it while the filing and delivery process is ongoing. All right. Yes, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. [B/C/S on English channel]. I can hear it from here. I can hear it from here. Let me say a few words [B/C/S on English channel]. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can hear no interpretation at present. The witness has no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it could be -- Usher, did you turn the volume completely down? I don't know. I mean -- can you hear now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Ms. Djilovic, can you hear me? I mean, can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's perfect. Two things: We started the ball rolling on your motion, even though it has not arrived. We don't know, of course, what the stand the Defence will be taking on it will be, so we are working on the assumption that it is the normal stand that you have taken in such instances as in the previous case we had. We're working on that assumption. But if -- whatever your position will be, of course it's -- we can't interfere with that. Please let us have it by the end of the day, if necessary -- if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, we're going to be looking at that. We will try and expedite that and look at certain issues during the next two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If Your Honours would allow us to file a very brief possibly courtesy copy with you by this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it would be better, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- and that could be formally filed tomorrow morning, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, that will be much better. Secondly, now let's go into private session for a short while, please, because I need to clear this up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. So, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Mrs. Djilovic, we were watching a video before the break. I would ask that you look at your monitor again. We are going to play the video through again, and then I will ask you some questions, and I will ask you, for expediency, for time's sake, we'll try and keep our answers limited, and I might have to on occasion stop you if you are giving an answer that appears to be quite lengthy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can we run the video again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the segment played from the video D1003 is -- starts at 00.00 to 01.59.8.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Djilovic, my question is do you agree that they were discussing at the meeting the military police?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discussion here was about Mirzet Halilovic, not about the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. So is it your testimony that what we just saw was not a discussion that was discussing the military police? You're saying no?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you agree --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about the military police but about Mirzet Halilovic personally. It was to do with the Potocari incident and Mirzet Halilovic who was there on paper and, I don't know but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mrs. Djilovic, I have to stop you here because I understand exactly what you have testified about before but I'd like you to concentrate on answering these questions. So the discussion we saw on the videotape was not about the military police. That's your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the discussion was about Mirzet Halilovic and the intervention or, rather, the incident that occurred at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, Mirzet Halilovic's name came up in the discussion. They talked about him. Didn't they also talk about the military police?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really -- I myself really cannot say that there was a military police in existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, it was not the military police. I'm only speaking on my own behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine. Let me ask another question concerning it. Would you agree that this videotape was also discussing the issue related to curfew?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were constant attempts at introducing a curfew. It was impossible, though, because people were living out in the streets. This idea of a curfew was never implemented simply because it was impossible to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. So while there might be discussions about curfew, you would agree it would be difficult to implement or enforce a curfew, correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was the desire to introduce a curfew. This was not just an idea, there were also decisions to that effect, but they could not have been implemented. There were many people who stayed outdoors, in the parks, on the streets. Had it been possible, it probably would have been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I will come back to that --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this was not just an idea that was raised once but on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. An important issue for the War Presidency. That would be your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was also important for the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you also agree that in this videotape they were discussing the fact of Mirzet Halilovic beating people?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the incident at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He beat up a lad and that's why he was chased away, together with his men, and that was the motive for summoning -- for scheduling the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me for cutting you off. We understand some of your testimony from direct. Now, you would also agree that on the videotape they were discussing incidents that happened in Potocari, and they said that the representative from Potocari was there.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what was said. There was a representative from Potocari. I heard him say so. Could you clarify your question? I did hear him say that there was a representative from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That was my question, ma'am. Do you know who the representative from Potocari was?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't. I don't know what he meant to say when he said a representative from Potocari. I -- I didn't understand. There was nothing else that he said that would clarify this to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you also agree that within the videotape there was discussion concerning an agreement made with Naser Oric? They said Naser agreed.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I be played this part --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that the gentleman said concerning Naser?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to be able to give you an accurate answer, I have to see and hear this again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we need to do that. And I suggest we start at the beginning and go through it. It's two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you see that portion of the video? Now, my question is, and you would agree, that they're discussing an agreement or something that Naser Oric agreed to in this video?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only heard him say, and probably everybody heard the same, "I told Naser Oric." Now, what he had told him or what he meant to say by saying that, I don't know. I only heard him say, "I told Naser Oric." I cannot comment upon it any further because I don't know what he meant when he said that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did he also say, "And Naser agreed"?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that as well, but I don't know what it was that Naser agreed with. I wasn't even supposed to know those things. I was a technical secretary, and I explained yesterday what my duties were. I'm sorry that I'm not able to give you any further information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers. We would like to see again that portion of -- that segment of the video that we have just seen, without interruptions, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Madam Djilovic, would you agree that in here the discussion that they're speaking of, they agreed, "I told Naser Oric," is about the military police?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that they were talking about the police. The person said, "The police came," and so on and so forth. It is possible that they were discussing the military police, but it was only on paper. In reality, in practice, it did not work properly. The fact that it existed on paper was an expression of the desire to have the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then one other question concerning this issue on the video. You agree that that was Mr. Avdic who was talking when reference was made to Naser?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be on the safe side, could I be shown the video clip again to see who is the speaker, because I only heard the voice. I'd like to see the face.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, president of the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I would like you to once again look at this video, and as you're looking at the video, I would like you to concentrate on how many persons are present with writing material, meaning paper or pencils. Can we show it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Djilovic, did the War Presidency supply them with the paper, or did those men bring paper or notebooks with them to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I don't think the War Presidency had supplies to spare to give them. Everybody was trying to get by, as regards the material, to try and find for themselves. I know that the War Presidency did not have enough paper. I have said that we were rummaging cabinets for paper, and whatever we were able to find was in very small quantities, quite insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know where they get the -- where they got the paper from.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. But a significant number of men in the room appeared to have paper or notebooks and pencils. Yes or no, Ms. Djilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, most of them had a piece of paper in front of them. I wasn't real little paying attention to pencils or pens, but most of them had some paper in front of them. This was a meeting, and it was only normal for them to have a piece of paper to make notes from the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question: In terms of Resid Efendic, did you note in the video that he was taking -- it appeared that he was writing on a notebook during this discussion.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Resid Efendic was secretary of the municipal War Presidency. He kept the minutes from this meeting. I said so yesterday, and I stand by what I said because this is how it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. I would now like to ask you one or two questions about Mirzet Halilovic. You testified about the incident of him beating persons up. Was Mirzet Halilovic a person who, when he drank, would become violent? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When intoxicated, he was a totally different person. That was the reason why he was removed from the police altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, this was known in the month of August that Mirzet Halilovic would beat people up and would become violent. You'd agree with me; right?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He beat people, including the Muslims. He did not distinguish between people when drunk. This was an object of discussion very often. He himself was sorry about his condition, he did not wish to be that way, but he drank and then acted the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And people who were members or who attended meetings of the War Presidency were aware that Mirzet Halilovic would become violent at times?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before he was admitted on the police force, they did not know of this nature of his. They probably would not have admitted it had they known. In general, he was a decent lad, a sportsman. He must have been affected by the war. That must have been the reason why he started drinking and being violent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, by August when this video was taken, it was known to members of the War Presidency that Mirzet Halilovic could be a violent person. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think we need to know whether the question is confined to the members of the War Presidency in that meeting where this discussion took place or whether Ms. Sellers is asking this witness whether she knows that every member of the War Presidency knew of this feature of Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a fair objection or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, Your Honour, we can break the question down in two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The members of the War Presidency who were present at this meeting knew that Mirzet Halilovic could have tendencies of being violent. Yes or no, Ms. Djilovic.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether all of them knew. I did not go about asking them whether they knew of him being violent, but probably the meeting itself was scheduled in order to inform them thereof and to talk about the entire matter and possibly about his replacement. His behaviour must have been the motive for this meeting, so even those who hadn't known about this prior to the meeting must have learnt about it at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you also agree that people in Potocari, from what we can gather by this video, probably also knew of the beating incident that Mirzet Halilovic was involved in?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the people in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not know. I didn't have any contacts with the people over there, and I really have no way of knowing what they thought. I'm sorry that I'm not able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you agree, from looking at that video, that the military police that went to Potocari during this incident were probably aware that Mirzet Halilovic was violent in the very least on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, it's simply that in answering the question of whether it was military police or Mirzet Halilovic, the witness's only spoke of Mirzet Halilovic, so this question assumes that there were other members of the military police, which the witness has denied, so I think it's going to be difficult for her to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, she hasn't actually denied but I don't think she was specifically asked as to whether -- we're talking about just one individual there in Potocari or more than one individual. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps if that's clarified, that would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we need to clarify that first and then we'll move -- yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would suggest that we might have to play --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's important. Because if it's not important, let's move forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- play the video again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what the video says is one thing. What the witness says is another.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, the witness -- I don't want to discuss the characterisation of her evidence but the witness has indicated certain things about the military police as related to this video, and my question is:

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Madam Djilovic, if you know, do you know whether the military police was aware that Mirzet Halilovic was a violent person, that members of the military police were aware that Mirzet Halilovic was a violent person?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't know that there was a unit of the military police, that it existed, so I cannot tell you whether members of the unit knew of this. I assert again that the military police in the strict sense of the term did not exist, only on paper. There were -- these were men who also worked in the civilian police. To put it simply, the military police did not exist. There may have been attempts at constituting one, like by terming it, calling it that way. I don't know of any military police. I know of the police that worked at the public security station and that they all worked together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm going to have to try and limit you so we'll be able to finish your testimony today. So my last question on this issue: So would it be your testimony that Mirzet Halilovic violent behaviour was not common knowledge? Is that what your testimony would be?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would they have scheduled the meeting unless it became known that he was violent? He wasn't violent otherwise, only when he was drunk, and that's why the meeting was scheduled, in order to solve the Mirzet Halilovic problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the last two questions were really invitations -- was really inviting the witness to speculate what the police knew, what the people of Potocari knew.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot know what someone thought of this or that. I can only tell you what I myself saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. My attention --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This places me in an uncomfortable position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My attention is being drawn by the Victims and Witnesses Unit. They wish to know whether they can -- whether we need the next witness here or whether we can send him back to the hotel for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'll try and finish with this witness today. I do not believe that we will be able to start with another witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you share that assessment, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not opposed to the idea to start the examination of the witness tomorrow, but I would really wish this witness to finish her testimony today, because the Victims and Witnesses Section informed me that the witness doesn't really feel well, that she would like to go home today, and I would really like my learned friends to keep this in mind, and I will keep that in mind for my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Victims and -- VWS section can take the next witness to the hotel, and we will proceed and tentatively do our best to finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's certainly my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both, Ms. Vidovic and Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask now that Prosecution Exhibit P590 be placed before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, if you would look at the document. I believe it is in Sanction but also I think there's a copy on the ELMO next to you. It's a document Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina military police station Srebrenica, list of military police staff. The first person on the list is Mirzet Halilovic. If you would turn to the second page, you will see that at the end of the list it says, "commander of the military police, Mirzet Halilovic," and then there's a date, Srebrenica, 31st July, 1992. Now, I would ask you to look at this document and to please tell the Trial Chamber now, after seeing this document, would it still be your testimony that there were no other police officers, military police members, that were in the Srebrenica municipality in the end of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my earlier statement. I find this list quite incredible that we had as many police officers. This list contains some deletions. Something was added. I really cannot comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can you comment --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone could have drafted this. I'm really sorry, I'm not able to give you an answer. The list could have been drawn at a later stage. It could have been typed, retyped, added or altered. I've never seen it before. That's why I cannot comment on it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Djilovic, when you're saying the list could have been typed, retyped, added, altered, this is speculation on your part, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, that's my question.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't said that. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to the next question, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not said speculations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, ma'am, you didn't say speculations. That is precisely my question to you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I just want to draw your attention to number 61 on the list, Sead Ademovic. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can I also draw your attention to number 15 on the list, Selahudin Omerovic.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you worked for Judge Omerovic in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, not from the very start. I worked there in late 1993. I didn't work there the entire 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Judge Omerovic had a cousin who also was living in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't. I worked only with Judge Omerovic, and I know him only. Believe me, I didn't have the time to get to know his relatives. I had my own family. I had my parents to attend to. I had to visit my parents, go back to my home and find food, fuel. I didn't have time to even see relatives. I wasn't even interested in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, Judge Eser would like to know what was the first name of Judge Omerovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It was Mensud, I believe, Your Honour, Mensud Omerovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mensud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
